title: FDR wins a third term
quote: I think you will find me in the future just exactly the same Franklin Roosevelt that you have known for a great many years.
quoteBy: Franklin D. Roosevelt, election night remarks to neighbors at Hyde Park, 1940

facts.text: On 5 November 1940 Franklin D. Roosevelt won an unprecedented third term as president, defeating Republican Wendell Willkie.
Roosevelt won 449 electoral votes to Willkie's 82.
He took about 27.3 million popular votes, about 54.7 percent, and carried 38 of the 48 states.
Roosevelt spent election night at his home in Hyde Park, New York, tallying returns.
Hundreds of neighbors marched up to the house with a fife and drum corps and flares, and Roosevelt came out onto the porch with his wife Eleanor, his mother Sara and his son Franklin Jr.
Speaking off the cuff, he told them, "We face difficult days in this country," and promised he would be the same Franklin Roosevelt they had always known.
The war shaped the race: the Battle of Britain had just ended on 31 October, and in September Roosevelt had signed the first peacetime draft in American history.
Willkie conceded by telegram the next day and wished Roosevelt health and happiness.
Weeks later Roosevelt proposed Lend Lease, and he signed the Lend Lease Act on 11 March 1941 to send arms to Britain.
Roosevelt went on to win a fourth term in 1944; no other president has been elected more than twice.

photoNote: Franklin D. Roosevelt speaks into microphones from his car, surrounded by crowds, during the 1940 campaign. NARA 79-XAR-9, public domain. From the campaign, not election night; no public domain photo of election night 1940 at Hyde Park was found (the FDR Library torchlight parade photos are from 1944). Quote check: the American Presidency Project has no transcript of these remarks, so the quote is verified word for word against the Evening Star staff report of 6 November 1940, page 2, which TIME matches; the United Press and AP versions differ slightly (listed in the slate).
photoCredit: Franklin D. Roosevelt speaks from his car during the 1940 campaign. NARA 79-XAR-9, public domain.

declassified.fact: Willkie did not stay a rival for long. In January 1941 he flew to Britain carrying a handwritten letter from Roosevelt to Churchill, dated 20 January, the day of the third inauguration. It quoted Longfellow's lines beginning "Sail on, O Ship of State." Churchill read the verse aloud in a broadcast weeks later.

body:
"We face difficult days in this country." Then the first president elected to a third term made his neighbors a promise.

5 November 1940. Franklin D. Roosevelt beat Wendell Willkie, 449 electoral votes to 82, carrying 38 of the 48 states. He spent election night at home in Hyde Park, New York, tallying returns.

Hundreds of neighbors marched up to the house with a fife and drum corps and flares. Roosevelt came out onto the porch with Eleanor, his mother Sara and his son Franklin Jr., and spoke off the cuff:

"I think you will find me in the future just exactly the same Franklin Roosevelt that you have known for a great many years."

The Battle of Britain had just ended. Weeks later, he proposed Lend Lease.
